title: How Colombia funds reconstruction after natural disasters
seoTitle: How Colombia funds reconstruction after natural disasters
subtitle: From the 1999 earthquake to the 2010‑2011 winter, the Colombian state resorted to taxes and special funds
excerpt: Natural disasters in Colombia generate billions in costs; governments create funds and raise temporary taxes to finance reconstruction and spur recovery.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
On August 10, 2026, the report revisits how Colombia has been handling the financial side of major natural catastrophes. The tragedies cause destruction of homes, commerce and infrastructure, demanding considerable state resources.

Economic impact of disasters

The 1999 Eje Cafetero earthquake, magnitude 6.4, caused estimated damages of about $1.857 billion, equivalent to 2.2 % of the national GDP at the time. The 2010‑2011 winter season affected 28 of the 32 departments, left more than 2.3 million people displaced and generated economic losses of 11.2 trillion pesos, roughly 2 % of GDP in that period.

Reconstruction fund for the Eje Cafetero

After the 1999 quake, Andrés Pastrana’s government declared an economic emergency and created the Fund for the Reconstruction and Social Development of the Eje Cafetero (Forec). This fund took charge of managing resources allocated for repairing the affected areas.

Taxes used after the 1999 earthquake

To raise funds, a 2 ‰ tax on financial transactions was introduced, initially temporary, which later remained in place and was increased to 4 ‰. In addition, income‑tax exemptions were granted to companies that set up in the affected zones, as well as tariff and VAT exemptions for importing reconstruction machinery and materials.

Measures adopted in the 2010‑2011 season

Under Juan Manuel Santos’s administration, the state postponed the removal of the 4 ‰ tax – already established by law – preserving this revenue source. It also expanded the tax base to include wealth and introduced a 25 % surcharge for taxpayers already paying this levy. Deductions for asset losses, changes in the calculation method of certain taxes, and special deadlines for fiscal obligations were offered. At the same time, the Adaptation Fund was created to finance reconstruction projects.

Recurring tax strategy

The examined episodes reveal a consistent response pattern: the adoption of temporary taxes, exemptions and fiscal benefits, together with the allocation of resources from the national budget, aims not only to cover the immediate emergency costs but also to stimulate production recovery and economic reactivation in the affected regions. Thus, the disaster’s financial impact extends beyond the day of the event, representing a prolonged expense for the Colombian state.

With information from El Tiempo.
